<reason>PRO set a clean decision rule in the opening (name a rival that is both better and achievable) and then sprang a trap that held for the rest of the debate: CON's "rights-first confederation" presupposes two sovereignties, so it is a two-state variant, not a rival to the motion. CON's own answer to the Ariel pressure question — "Palestinian police, under Palestinian law" — effectively conceded sovereign Palestinian jurisdiction over Israeli residents, which PRO correctly framed as the motion by another road. CON's closing reframe ("PRO surrendered the content of partition") is rhetorically sharp but only works if the motion requires hard-border evacuation, which it does not; and once confederation is inside the two-state tent, CON has no remaining rival and never seriously contested PRO's claim that the truly achievable alternatives (permanent control, managed conflict) are worse. CON did land real damage on achievability — the "several Gazas" residual, the thrice-rejected swap map, the hypothetical package — and its "recognition vote vs. civil war" comparison was its best material, keeping the debate competitive. But PRO answered both pressure questions directly with A1/A2, offered a coherent falsification test, and gave the judge the simpler path: CON's plan asks more of the same Knesset and has never had a constituency. Minor demerit to PRO for saying CON's Ariel answer "never came" before CON had its turn.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2 ("who arrests the settler in Ariel — Palestinian police or the IDF?") and the follow-through: CON answered "Palestinian police, under Palestinian law," and PRO's closing converted that into a concession that CON's rival is itself a two-state outcome, collapsing CON's route to victory.</best_rebuttal>
